title: Introduction to Big O Notation
description: Understand what Big O notation is and why it is important in algorithm analysis

blocks.text: Big O Notation is a way to measure how efficiently your code performs as the input size grows.
You've probably seen code that works perfectly on small inputs but slows down, crashes, or times out when the input becomes large.
Understanding Big O helps you avoid slow, inefficient solutions and write code that actually scales.
It's also one of the most important topics in coding interviews.
You'll almost always be asked to explain the time and space complexity of your solution and the more efficient your approach, the stronger your chances of passing the interview.
In this chapter, I'll break down:
Let's get started.
So… what exactly is Big O Notation?
Big O is a mathematical way to describe how the performance of an algorithm changes as the size of the input grows.
It doesn't tell you the exact time your code will take.
Instead, it gives you a high-level growth trend how fast the number of operations increases relative to the input size.
For example: if your input doubles, does your algorithm take twice as long? Ten times as long? Or does it barely change at all?
Big O helps you answer those questions without even running the code so you can choose the most efficient algorithm for large inputs.
Below is a rough visualization of how time grows with input size n:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785248993301-338694828.png
One important thing to note Big O is machine-independent.
It doesn't matter whether your code runs on a fast laptop or a slow server. The growth pattern stays the same.
The key variable that drives Big O is the input size (N). As N increases, Big O helps you predict whether the algorithm will still be efficient or become impractical.
Now that you understand what Big O Notation is, let's go over the most common time complexities you'll encounter.
Even small differences in complexity like O(n) vs O(n log n) make a huge impact as n grows.
1. Constant Time O(1)
This is the fastest and most efficient time complexity.
An algorithm is O(1) if it performs a fixed number of operations meaning the execution time does not depend on the size of the input.
A classic example is simply checking whether a number is even or odd:
It doesn't matter if n is 5 or 5 billion the operation is always a single step. No looping, no scanning. Just one direct check.
How it flows:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785248994832-228696492.png
2. Logarithmic Time O(log n)
Next up is logarithmic time, or O(log n).
An algorithm runs in O(log n) when every step reduces the problem size by half. This means the amount of work grows very slowly even when the input becomes massive.
The most common example is Binary Search:
Instead of checking every element one by one, you jump directly to the middle and eliminate half of the array in a single step. Then you repeat the same process on the remaining half.
To put that into perspective, here are the number of steps binary search takes for different input sizes:

codes.javascript:
Input size = 8              →  max 3 steps
Input size = 1,000          →  max 10 steps
Input size = 1,000,000      →  max 20 steps
Input size = 1,000,000,000  →  just 30 steps!

blocks.text: Even with a billion elements, binary search takes only 30 steps.
How it flows:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785248996298-965867353.png
3. Linear Time O(n)
Now let's talk about Linear Time, or O(n).
An algorithm is O(n) when its running time grows directly in proportion to the input size. If the input doubles, the number of operations also doubles.
A simple example is finding the largest number in an array:
You start with the first element and walk through every single one comparing as you go. There's no shortcut every element must be checked at least once.
With 10 elements you do 10 comparisons. With 1 million, you do 1 million.
How it flows:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785248997828-832444560.png
Other common O(n) examples include summing all values in an array, printing every item in a linked list, or traversing all nodes in a tree.
In general whenever your algorithm must visit each element at least once, you're dealing with O(n).
4. Linearithmic Time O(n log n)
Now we enter the world of O(n log n) also called linearithmic time.
Algorithms with O(n log n) combine two behaviors:

items: A log n factor from repeatedly splitting the input in half
An n factor from processing every element at each level

blocks.text: It's often described as: logarithmic splitting with linear merging.
The classic example is Merge Sort:

First it keeps splitting the array in half that's the log n part. Then at every level it merges all pieces back together, touching every element that's the n part. Multiply them and you get O(n log n).
How it flows:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785248999348-834804889.png
This complexity is slightly slower than pure linear, but still very efficient — and it's the backbone of many fast sorting algorithms used in production today.
5. Quadratic Time O(n²)
Next up quadratic time, or O(n²). This is where things start to get ugly.
In an O(n²) algorithm, the number of operations grows proportionally to the square of the input size. This typically happens when you have a loop running inside another loop.
A straightforward example is Bubble Sort:
The outer loop runs n times. The inner loop also runs up to n times for each outer step. That gives you n × n operations.
How it flows:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785249000926-128332868.png
Here's how badly the numbers scale:
These algorithms are fine for small inputs, but painfully slow as n grows. In interviews you'll almost always want to find a way to bring O(n²) down to something better.
6. Exponential Time O(2ⁿ)
Exponential time algorithms usually appear when we try to solve a problem by checking every possible combination often through recursion or backtracking.
Think of it as the opposite of binary search. Instead of eliminating half the work at each step, you're often doubling the work with each extra element added to the input.
A classic example is the recursive Fibonacci sequence:
Each call branches into two more calls. Those two each branch into two more. The tree of calls doubles at every level.
How it flows:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785249002364-632853668.png
Just increasing the input size from n = 20 to n = 30 causes the number of calls to jump from about a million to roughly a billion.

The good news is that many exponential-time problems can be dramatically improved using memoization or dynamic programming. These techniques avoid recomputing the same subproblems repeatedly, often reducing the time complexity to O(n).
7. Factorial Time O(n!)
And finally the most explosive time complexity of them all: factorial time, or O(n!).
This occurs when an algorithm tries every possible arrangement (permutation) of n elements.
A classic example is generating all permutations of an array:
For each position, you try every remaining element. Then recurse. Then undo. The possibilities explode instantly.
How it flows:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785249003903-13686956.png

These kinds of brute-force solutions are only usable for very small inputs. For anything larger, smarter techniques like dynamic programming, branch-and-bound, or heuristics are used to cut the search space down drastically.
So far we've focused on time complexity how fast an algorithm runs as input size grows.
But Big O also applies to memory usage and that is called space complexity.
In interviews, you'll often be asked to analyze both time and space complexity. Because in real systems, performance isn't just about speed. It's also about how much memory your solution consumes.
Space complexity tells you how much extra memory your algorithm uses in addition to the input itself.
This extra memory can come from:

items: Temporary data structures like arrays, hash maps, stacks, queues

blocks.text: Even if your algorithm is fast, it may still waste memory which can be a serious problem in large-scale systems or environments with limited RAM.
Now let's look at the most common space complexities you will come across:
O(1) Constant Space
Only a fixed number of variables are used, no matter how large the input is.
Just one variable total. The array size doesn't change the memory footprint at all.
O(n) Linear Space
A new structure is created that grows with the input.
If the input has n elements, the copy also has n elements. Space scales directly with input size.
O(n²) Quadratic Space
Storing a full n × n grid or matrix takes O(n²) space like an adjacency matrix for a graph with n nodes.
Space from Recursion O(h), O(n), or worse
Space complexity isn't only about the extra data structures you create. Recursion also consumes memory through the call stack and this often goes unnoticed.
Every recursive call adds a new frame to the stack until the function returns.
For DFS on a balanced tree, the stack depth equals the height O(log n) space. On a skewed tree where every node only has one child, it becomes O(n).
Now let's talk about how to actually calculate the complexity of any piece of code.
The simplest way is to break your code down into parts and analyze each part separately.
Rule 1. Add Complexities of Sequential Blocks
If your algorithm performs one block of work after another, add their complexities:
Rule 2 Multiply Complexities of Nested Blocks
If you have a loop inside another loop, multiply their complexities:
Rule 3. Drop Constant Factors
Big O describes how an algorithm grows as the input size increases not the exact number of operations. Constants don’t change the overall growth trend, so we drop them.
Rule 4. Drop Lower-Order Terms
Keep only the term that grows the fastest. As the input size becomes very large, the slower-growing terms become insignificant.

codes.javascript:
O(n² + n)      →  O(n²)
O(n³ + n²)     →  O(n³)
O(2ⁿ + n¹⁰⁰)  →  O(2ⁿ)

blocks.text: At n = 1,000,000 the n² term towers so far above n that the lower term contributes essentially nothing. So you keep the dominant one and move on.
Now that you understand what Big O Notation means and how to calculate it, there's an important nuance worth addressing.
Big O gives us an upper bound it tells us the worst-case growth rate. But not every input triggers that worst-case behavior. Some inputs make an algorithm fly. Others bring it to its knees.
That's exactly where Best, Worst, and Average Case Complexity comes in a more complete way to describe how an algorithm truly behaves across all kinds of inputs.
In the next chapter, we'll explore what these three cases mean, how to identify them, and why they matter when analyzing real-world algorithms.
